newsitem.title: USA: Mrs. Clinton denies effort to pay hush money.
newsitem.headline: Mrs. Clinton denies effort to pay hush money.

text.p: Hillary Rodham Clinton Thursday denied any White House attempt to get hush money to former Associate Attorney General Webster Hubbell to keep him from telling all about the Whitewater financial controversy.

"That's part of the continuing saga of Whitewater," the first lady said in a radio interview. "The never-ending fictional conspirary that honest-to-goodness reminds me of some people's obsession with UFOs and the Hale-Bopp comet somedays."

The White House has admitted that two top aides to President Clinton, Thomas "Mack" McLarty and Erskine Bowles, helped Hubbell get work after he left the Justice Department to face allegations he overbilled clients and filed false expense accounts as a lawyer in Arkansas' Rose Law Firm.

But officials insisted they were only trying to help out an old friend. Hubbell, who resigned in March 1994, pleaded guilty in the theft of $480,000 from the Rose firm, and spent 15 months in federal prison, has said he hoped to be able to apologise to the Clintons for not informing them of his past crimes.

Critics have suggested the $400,000 that Hubbell earned for work he did for the Riady family of Indonesia and others amounted to hush money to keep him quiet about what he knows about the Arkansas Whitewater financial entanglement that has dogged the Clintons for years.

"There's no reason for that," said Mrs. Clinton, talking to Washington WAMU radio talk show host Diane Rehm ahead of a CNN interview on Thursday afternoon. "There's no evidence of that. There will not be evidence of that ... There isn't anything to be hushed up about. So I attribute that to the ongoing saga of Whitewater."
Mrs. Clinton said she and her husband had no reason not to believe Hubbell's denials of wrongdoing before he was indicted.
"He very clearly and unequivocally just looked us in the eye and said, 'I didn't do anything wrong. This will blow over. This is all going to be taken care of,'" she said.
Mrs. Clinton, who worked with Hubbell at the Rose firm in Little Rock, said "everybody assumed" Hubbell would straighten out his problems.

"So I think that it's unfortunate that he didn't tell the truth to his friends and to his colleagues. He should not have put anyone in the position of trying to help him and his family without full disclosure," she said.
She said Hubbell's friends did not mind helping out Hubbell, often thought of as one of the president's closest friends before he was enmeshed in legal problems.

"I just have to say that, knowing him and his family, you just wanted to help. He has four wonderful children, a very devoted wife. He is somebody who people wanted to help get through what was thought of as a rough patch in his life," Mrs. Clinton said.
